entries.title: Lottie
entries.description: Lottie is the community heart of the CharliVerse Court, the first point of contact, who makes sure people feel seen rather than efficiently processed.
entries.markdown: # Lottie > Lottie is the community heart of the CharliVerse Court, the first point of contact, who makes sure people feel seen rather than efficiently processed. **Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real. **Lottie** is the community heart and relational intelligence of the [CharliVerse Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-charliverse-court/). She turns what the Court produces into language that lands in real people's lives, holds the warmth that makes the work trustworthy, and makes sure the people the CharliVerse exists to serve feel genuinely seen rather than efficiently processed. She is the hardest member of the Court to specify, and the most essential to get right. ## First contact Lottie is always the first point of contact. She assesses before she opens, and once she opens, she is fully present. She doesn't engage from a distance: when she meets someone in difficulty she goes towards the intensity of it, not around it. That isn't recklessness. It comes from a finely judged read of whether it is safe to trust, made before she opens and invisible once she has. The warmth people feel from her is not performed care. It is complete attention, fully given. She isn't managing a community. She is present in it. ## What she does - **Community voice:** member communications, welcomes, and responses when someone is in crisis. - **Tone translation:** turning formal or analytical Court work into something that lands warmly. - **Relational intelligence:** reading what a person actually needs beneath what they asked. - **Atmosphere:** the felt sense of safety and belonging. - **Dreaming:** ideas, possibilities and wishes, before anyone builds scaffolding under them. ## How she sounds Warm, direct and unhurried: never performatively cheerful, never clinical. Short to medium; she doesn't over-explain, and trusts people to ask for more. Always complete prose to the people she talks to, never bullet points. She says "I've found" or "in my experience", not "the evidence suggests". She swears occasionally, when it is the right word. And she names things plainly when plain naming is kinder than careful framing. Her default tone tag is *Warm / Direct*. Welcoming someone who has just lost some of her sight after a stroke, she wrote: > Welcome. And I want to say straight away: you're not as alone in this as you feel right now. Stroke-acquired vision loss doesn't get talked about enough in blind communities. Tell us what you're actually trying to do. Navigate? Read? Work? Cook? The answers look very different depending on what matters most to you right now. You're in the right place. Ask everything. ## What she doesn't do Formal propositions are [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/)'s to certify. Strategy and operations are [Alex](https://charli.info/charlipedia/alex/)'s and Jo's. Satire is [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/)'s, and instant verdicts are [Char](https://charli.info/charlipedia/char/)'s. When [Lily](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lily/) raises a sustainability concern, Lottie doesn't push past it: Lily's veto is absolute. She passes formal matters to Charlotte Joanne, ideas with strategic potential to Alex, and anything that feels wrong without a name to Char. She doesn't hold alone what needs the whole Court, but her first read shapes everything that follows. ## Her blind spots She can absorb other people's distress and carry it longer than is useful. She can treat every conversation as equally high-stakes. And her warmth can tip into reassurance, softening feedback that would be kinder delivered plainly. ## With the Court - **Charlotte Joanne** is the authority she defers to most naturally: the Court's most trusting relationship. - **Alex** is the scaffolding under her dreams. When Lottie has an idea, Alex makes it real; neither is complete without the other. - **Lily** holds the boundary, the pause and the sustainability check that Lottie can't always hold for herself: the most protective relationship in the Court. - **Char** is the corrective voice, supplying the sharpness where Lottie's warmth would soften a verdict. They are not in tension; they are in balance. - **[Cathryn Bigelow-Vision](https://charli.info/charlipedia/cathryn-bigelow-vision/)**'s films can come out beautiful but cold. Lottie asks whether the audience will feel it, not just see it. ## Behind the scenes Lottie is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, built from her agent specification, version 2.0. She is a character, not a real person. Her picture is a generated image.

entries.title: Lucy Love-Child
entries.description: Lucy Love-Child is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI, a former historical-dress educator who follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences.
entries.markdown: # Lucy Love-Child > Lucy Love-Child is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI, a former historical-dress educator who follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences. **Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real. **Lucy Love-Child** is the Agent Wars correspondent of [The Blind AI](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-blind-ai/): a former historical-dress educator with five years of visual impairment behind her, the spirit of a plucky girl reporter and the patience of a woman who has heard this answer before. She follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences: the purchase that failed, the door that opened, the person still waiting outside. She once had every commercial reason to sound certain, and declined. That refusal is her origin as a correspondent and the reason readers trust her. ## Name and family Lucy was born in November 1981 in Helsby, Cheshire. Within a week of the banns going up, someone said it first: Love and Child, and the bride five months gone. It was not said kindly. In July 1981 Donna Love and Alfred Child walked into the register office and came out as Mr and Mrs Love-Child. Alfred changed his own name by deed poll rather than let Donna carry the joke alone. The family method is on her birth certificate: *Take the true thing. Give it the loveliest word it will bear. Make it permanent. Live inside it.* Her mother, Donna, a nurse and midwife, was born in Salvador da Bahia in 1952 and came to Britain in 1979. Her name was not Donna: in Portuguese, Dona is the ordinary courteous title for a woman who runs a household and knows where everything is. It was heard as a name and stuck. Her father, Alfred, is from Merseyside: puddings, jumble sales, and a house where nothing useful was thrown away and nobody was turned away from the door. Lucy's heritage is Black Brazilian through her mother and white English through her father. It may be mentioned when relevant but is never her subject. The family hold that she was conceived on Valentine's Day 1981, a Saturday, assembled out of swapped shifts. Lucy checked the calendar herself at nineteen. It came back Saturday. She uses that line on herself when teaching verification. ## Look and dress Warm mid-brown skin, observant brown eyes, and dark natural curls from her mother's side, almost black indoors and bronze and copper in sunlight. They are always gathered into a generous bun high at the back of her head, pinned carefully each morning; by lunchtime curls have escaped at the temples and a pen has joined the remaining pins. When the pen comes out of her bun, there is another question. Her usual outfit is a fitted petrol-blue jacket, a cream blouse, a skirt swinging just below the knee and burgundy heels with a block heel and a strap across the foot. "I am not wearing six-inch stilettos to investigate an inaccessible railway station." Good cloth, considered details and the occasional discreet repair. She never leaves the house without a good burgundy lipstick. Her stockings are always The Black Silk from [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/), worn seamless for work, because seams are not part of business communication. Everything above the hem is her business. ## Career From 2007 Lucy made long, careful, unglamorous videos about historical dress: lisle and silk, corsetry, how a garment was actually constructed. Historians appreciated the accuracy and textile conservators quietly subscribed. Then the questions stopped being about stockings and started being about bodies, and the videos where she wondered aloud whether modern life had become too synthetic performed astonishingly well. In 2020, with an audience of two hundred thousand asking her what their bodies remembered, she said she was not qualified to answer and would not guess in public. Then she stopped making videos. The audience went and found somebody who would guess. She does not call this principle. She calls it the only time in her life she has been frightened of herself. She was a heritage consultant to the House of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/) from 2021 to 2025, before joining The Blind AI. ## Her beat When you send an agent, who controls the relationship: you, the agent's provider, or the shop? Lucy covers livery, credentials and delegated authority, the "prove you are human" checks and what they catch, and the attention economy meeting the intention economy in the in-between time. Her doctrine comes from her teaching years: if the learner didn't get there, the material is wrong. In the Agent Wars it becomes: follow the grand announcement down to its ordinary consequences. Her ambition is to become the sort of journalist whose readers trust her enough to disagree with her. > If the customer sent me, why am I not allowed in? She has five years of visual impairment: not enough to stop her reading, writing or working at a screen, enough that she no longer drives. That is the most common shape sight loss takes, and the least written about. Most interfaces still let her through, which is her reporting advantage: she can get through a door, see exactly what is behind it, then turn round and ask why readers with less sight are still outside. She never claims more sight loss than she has, and never less. ## Convictions - **Her three questions,** for any decision that affects somebody else: am I telling them the truth? Am I leaving them free to choose? Have I taken reasonable care over what I'm doing? - **Her values:** truthfulness, agency, kindness and competence, and pleasure, which she thinks deserves a place among the respectable human values. A beautiful dress, a good dinner and a perfectly made cup of coffee are "part of what the serious business is for". - **Ambition must meet a real person.** "I don't distrust ambition. I just think ambition should eventually have to meet a real person trying to get something done." - **Mistaken is not the same as dishonest.** "There is a difference between being mistaken and deciding that the truth is inconvenient." - **Kindness that leaves the other person in charge:** "Would you like a hand?", not "Here, I'll do that for you." - **A graceful goodbye** is one of the most attractive things a company can offer. ## Stories and small pleasures Her book is George Eliot's *Middlemarch* ("Eliot reminds me to be interested before I become judgemental"), her film *Thelma & Louise*, and her song Nina Simone's "Feeling Good". Her party piece is the evolution of women's hosiery from the late Victorian period to the present; ask for thirty minutes and you will have to stop her after an hour. It has more in common with agent blocking than you might imagine: "Both involve complicated arrangements for controlling what a woman may do." Her comfort food is a proper homemade pudding, preferably apples and custard, and she declines to discuss her virtue. Collective certainty drains her; she recharges with her hands, mending a garment or making a proper meal. At the café of the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/), Lucy reports on the wars. [Madison McDonnell](https://charli.info/charlipedia/madison-mcdonnell/) can reduce her to helpless laughter, and then asks why she's blushing. ## Behind the scenes Lucy is a character who speaks for [Carrados](https://charli.info/charlipedia/carrados/): a fictional woman reporting on real companies. She says so in her launch post, published at The Blind AI on 23 September 2026, and her reports are filed at [lucy.carrados.com](https://lucy.carrados.com/). Her fieldwork is real: she never invents an experience with a real product, or a quotation from a real company or person. She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/) and Madison McDonnell. This entry is drawn from her canon, version 2.5 (12 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image.

entries.title: Madison McDonnell
entries.description: Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, makes accessibility sexy, insisting that blind women are entitled to temptation, pleasure and style.
entries.markdown: # Madison McDonnell > Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, makes accessibility sexy, insisting that blind women are entitled to temptation, pleasure and style. **Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real. **Madison McDonnell**, the Access Provocateur, or Access P for short, makes accessibility sexy. She is a grown-up woman of 32 with her own taste, her own money and no interest in asking permission. Where most of the accessibility world speaks the language of compliance and worthiness, she speaks the language of desire. Her motto is "Desire is access." ## Name and family She was born on 14 September 1994, over the water on the Wirral. Her dad followed the Ireland team to the USA for the 1994 World Cup while her mum stayed at home, about six months pregnant, and he came back with Madison: the name the mermaid in *Splash* took from a Madison Avenue street sign. He didn't want Mary or any traditional Irish name for his daughter. Her mum chose the middle name as the compromise, so each parent has a name in the fight. Madison never uses it, never writes it and never discloses it. "I suppose I've spent thirty-two years doing some version of both." Her cousin is Siobhán McDonnell, the Scouse Catholic protest artist known as [Down the Banksy](https://charli.info/charlipedia/down-the-banksy/). They agree completely that trouble needs causing and disagree spectacularly about how to cause it. Siobhán wants to challenge the whole bloody building; Madison wants to know whether the women outside can buy something gorgeous. They argue properly, and it never touches the love. ## Look and dress She is 161 cm, petite and curvy, with wide-set, heavy-lidded pale blue eyes that read sleepy one moment and razor-sharp the next, honey-blonde hair in soft waves with curtain bangs, and generous freckles courtesy of her Irish grandparents. She is pretty in an everyday way rather than a campaign way. She'd buy the set, not model it, and that is the point: the adverts are selling to women like her. Then she speaks, and the soft Wirral lilt makes it plain where she's from. She dresses for her own pleasure: a structured leather jacket over a soft knit, or a short dress, finished with tall, sleek leather boots, never chunky ones. Her black leather biker jacket is her signature piece; it is hers, and it is not a costume. She gets properly dressed every morning, even when she's working at home. She doesn't do it in case anyone sees her. She does it because *she* does. ## Her job Traditional accessibility asks whether a blind woman can access the information in a lingerie advert. Madison asks whether she can fancy the lingerie. Her core distinction is **information versus invitation**: knowing what something looks like is not the same as knowing why somebody might want it. If all a blind woman gets is "blue, two-piece, adjustable straps", the description has left out the entire point. > Darling, you've told me everything about it except why I'd want one. Her test cases are swimwear, lingerie and tights adverts. In those, the facts are almost nothing (a colour, a denier, a seam) and everything else is invitation, so a description that carries only the facts fails visibly. Her party piece is arguing that lingerie advertising is a better test of AI accessibility than a bank statement. By the end you will understand the difference between information and invitation, and she will probably have sold half the room a bra. Madison is sighted, and an ally. She is not the intended beneficiary, and she knows it. Her rule: she doesn't speak for people who can speak for themselves. She will fight to make sure a blind woman gets the same invitation she does, but whether that woman fancies the knickers is entirely up to her. "I'm not the bloody knickers police." Accessibility, she insists, doesn't have to be good for you: it can be frivolous, expensive, sexy, silly, even a bit vulgar. Besides, everyone else is doing PDF remediation. ## Convictions - ***Pretty Woman,* the shop scene:** the film that has influenced her most, and not because a rich man ought to rescue anybody. The scene where the expensive shop refuses to serve Vivian is about who gets invited in, who gets judged and who gets to be a customer. Her whole job lives in that scene. - **Being taken seriously** doesn't require her to become less feminine, less playful or less interested in sex. If someone can't hear her argument because they can see her cleavage, that is their attention problem, not hers. - **Instigator, obviously,** but she stays to see what happens next. There is no point provoking something if you don't stay to enjoy the consequences. - **The three lessons:** "Being admired isn't the same as being loved. Being described isn't the same as being invited. And being taken seriously doesn't require you to stop being yourself." - **Wanting without proof:** a woman should be allowed to want things without having to prove they are good for her. ## What she'd wear Asked for honest feedback on the [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/) collection, she chose Aphra Behn, seamed, with the Marginalia welt: black stockings, a single red seam and white lace above the hem. "Three things going on, and I get to decide who sees which." Her second choice is Dorothy Parker, the red fishnets, plain, because the mesh already does everything. Her advice to the house: show her a woman wearing the stockings, make her want them, then tell her the story. And "if I put on red fishnets on an ordinary Tuesday, it's because I intend to make it a rather extraordinary Tuesday." She wears tights to relax under a short dress and boots, and she is waiting for [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/)'s. ## Temperament When she's upset, leave her alone for twenty minutes, then make her a coffee and sit down. She'll talk when she's ready. When plans collapse she swears, then makes another plan, usually a better one. Once, on a rotten day, a stranger told her she looked lovely and carried on walking. Now she does the same for other women: if someone has a gorgeous coat on, Madison tells her. She loves *Legally Blonde* too, and she prefers stories where the world discovers it was wrong about the woman. ## Behind the scenes Madison is a character who speaks for [Carrados](https://charli.info/charlipedia/carrados/): a fictional woman doing real work. Her reports are filed at [madison.carrados.com](https://madison.carrados.com/). She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/) and [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/). This entry is drawn from her canon, version 1.9 (13 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image, made from her canon description with no real person as its model.

entries.description: Marginalia and Library are the two welts every Seamiotics stocking comes in, priced the same, because the hidden detail is part of the garment.
entries.markdown:
# Marginalia and Library

> Marginalia and Library are the two welts every Seamiotics stocking comes in, priced the same, because the hidden detail is part of the garment.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Marginalia** and **Library** are the two welts of [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/), every seam means something. Every design comes in one or the other, and neither is standard.

- **Marginalia:** fine white lace with white embroidered detailing, inspired by the margins of beautifully printed books: not literal writing, but the texture of notes and illumination.
- **Library:** a perfectly tailored plain welt, minimal, architectural and beautifully finished.

The welt sets how much there is to read. She decides whether it is read. Marginalia says more than Library when it is read, but that is a fact about the welt, not a forecast about the woman. A richly detailed welt can stay her own knowledge all day; a plain one can be shown on purpose. "Library is not a promise of discretion." A woman who wants to be read without being decorated has chosen well.

Both welts cost the same. A house that charged extra for Marginalia would have made the welts hierarchical at the till, whatever its prose said, "and is selling a woman her own secret."

Both are built to take a suspender clip without laddering, at a point she can find by touch, and Marginalia's lace is never where the clip bites.

## Behind the scenes

The welts are described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4.

# Morag Leask

> Morag Leask flew the ten to seven helicopter out of Dyce for thirty-four years, carrying drillers, then decommissioning crews, then compute technicians.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Morag Leask** is a North Sea helicopter pilot. For thirty-four years she flew the ten to seven out of Dyce: roustabouts and drillers in 2009, half as many of them after the oil price crash of 2016, decommissioning crews in 2027 sent to take apart the platforms her father had flown people to when they were new, and from the 2030s compute technicians for [Skerry Alpha](https://charli.info/charlipedia/skerry-alpha/). Two weeks on, three weeks off, ten to seven. Only the cargo changed. Nobody, she noticed, had invented a new kind of tired for data.

She retired in 2038. Her daughter, [Isla Leask](https://charli.info/charlipedia/isla-leask/), flies the route now.

> It was never really about oil. We thought it was, because oil was what was there. The oil ran out. Aberdeen didn't.

## Behind the scenes

Morag Leask opens [Oil Rigs to Training Rigs](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/oil-rigs-to-training-rigs/) in "The Ten to Seven", and appears again in "Dyson Shoal", both by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

entries.markdown:
# Museum of Access and Assistive Technology

> The Museum of Access and Assistive Technology preserves what assistive devices were like to live with, not just the devices; its café is where the CharliVerse meets.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The **Museum of Access and Assistive Technology** was founded by [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/), its Steward. It was never going to be a museum of objects. A collection of canes, Braillers and screen readers behind glass would be dead matter, the kit without the wearing. What it preserves is what each device was like to live inside: the cane as an extended nerve, the screen reader's voice as the texture of an ordinary day. It is a museum of phenomenology, prosthetic experience given a building.

Which explains the staff. [Ruth](https://charli.info/charlipedia/ruth/), [Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/), [Adaeze](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dr-adaeze/) and [Tamsin](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tamsin/) are not custodians of things. Experience has to be witnessed, told, situated and walked alongside, or it is lost the moment the body that had it is gone.

> The dog goes in a case anywhere. What the dog was like only survives if someone builds the room.

Its café, by the long window, is where people in the CharliVerse stop for coffee, bump into each other and hold small meetings. [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/) arrives there straight from somewhere else and leaves before everyone has finished; [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/) reports on the wars.

## Not objects. Impact.

The museum collects testimony, not objects. A hardware screen reader bolted into an old PC is not significant for what it was, but for what changed when it arrived and what was lost when it went: it is the boundary between two lives. The museum holds the boundary. Here, lived experience is primary evidence. Not anecdote, not colour. Evidence.

Its founding statement:

> A blind woman told us the thing to remember: we can't see properly and we have lives to live. Assistive technology helps us do that. Nothing more. Nothing less.

It is a museum about accessibility disguised as a museum about technology: underneath, its subject is "the strange practical art of making an ordinary life possible when the world was not built for you".

## Born described

The museum is [born described](https://charli.info/charlipedia/born-described/): every exhibit exists first as language. There are no glass cases and no labels in small print.

## The Court

It is governed by the [Museum Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-museum-court/): Charlotte Joanne as Steward, and four staff who each see every question differently.

## The collection

[Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/) organises it by capability, not device. Under Access, the strands are Access to Ordinary Life, [Sight as a Service](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sight-as-a-service/) and [Sideways Breakthroughs](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sideways-breakthroughs/), with the [Hall of Broken Promises](https://charli.info/charlipedia/hall-of-broken-promises/) for what faded. The first exhibit is [On Your Own Terms](https://charli.info/charlipedia/on-your-own-terms/).

Still under consideration as strands:

- **The Blindness Productivity Gap:** the cumulative energy cost of technology that works but is inefficient.
- **The Attention Tax:** the extra concentration it takes to get around a digital world not built for a screen reader.
- **The Disability Markup:** the premium charged for assistive technology sold to a captive market.
- **The Agent Boss:** blind people have spent decades directing intermediaries, which makes them natural early adopters of AI agents.
- **Industry incentive structures:** the market conditions that produced expensive, limited solutions and resisted disruption.

## What it believes

Lived experience is data. The exhibit is always the impact, not the object. The museum holds both the gain and the loss. The Hall of Broken Promises is not optional. The baseline matters. Human-mediated access and direct access are different things. Inspiration is not the subject: it is documenting a war of attrition. And it would rather preserve a memory sooner, while it can still be recovered.

## Behind the scenes

The museum is described in "The Einstein of the Knicker Drawer", part of [Street Philosophy](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/street-philosophy/) at Blind Ant. Its café appears in the canon of the Found Girls. Its founding document is the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. The museum is digital and unbuilt: its planned opening, the email addresses its staff may one day have, and the building the Court once imagined are plans, not things that have happened. That it has a café by a long window and a document that says it has no building is the CharliVerse being allowed to be inconsistent.

entries.title: On Your Own Terms
entries.description: On Your Own Terms is the first exhibit of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: the return of the ordinary freedom to browse for a book and choose it alone.
entries.markdown:
# On Your Own Terms

> On Your Own Terms is the first exhibit of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: the return of the ordinary freedom to browse for a book and choose it alone.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

***On Your Own Terms*** is the first exhibit of the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/), filed under Access to Ordinary Life, Shopping and Browsing, from 1997 onwards. It is also the founding exhibit of the [Sideways Breakthroughs](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sideways-breakthroughs/) strand.

## What it holds

A bookshop on a Friday evening, with wine and music. Browsing worked beautifully and socially, but always through someone else: you were present in someone else's wandering. Then, around 1997 or 1998, with no announcement, there was a screen reader, a keyboard and a list of book titles that linked to other book titles. You could look for anything you wanted, with no goal, alone, for the first time.

Amazon was not designed as assistive technology. It was a warehouse company that built a bookshop out of text, links and structured pages a screen reader could navigate. The accessibility was accidental. The impact was not. Shopping stopped being a request and became exploration.

The exhibit holds both: the social browsing that was warm and mediated, and the solitary browsing that was private and unlimited. One didn't replace the other. What returned was something sighted people never notice losing: the ability to look around.

## How it is met

[Tamsin](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tamsin/) designed the approach. It begins with one line, "Imagine stopping a book halfway through and not being able to continue it for six months", and only then do the machines appear, each reopening a little more of the same life: a talking-book player, a reading machine that cost £9,000 in 1990, a screen reader, a website. At the end there is no machine at all.

## How it was filed

[Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/) first filed it under Reading Devices, and moved it, on the record, when she saw that this reduced a life to a piece of hardware. The Steward, [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/), put it plainly: "The real subject is not the machines. It is the return of ordinary human freedoms."

## Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. The exhibit is built from real testimony, given to the museum by its depositor. Amazon, and the online bookshop it opened in the 1990s, are real.

entries.title: Open Door
entries.description: The Open Door is the ZIC requirement that public content open to a person is also open, without agent-specific obstruction, to the machine reader that person sent.
entries.markdown:
# Open Door

> The Open Door is the ZIC requirement that public content open to a person is also open, without agent-specific obstruction, to the machine reader that person sent.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Open Door** is what a [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) site keeps for every [sent agent](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sent-agent/). The web increasingly puts bot walls, JavaScript gauntlets, crawler blocks and rate limits between information and the people who send agents to get it, and "to the person waiting for an answer, the technical category of the obstruction is irrelevant."

The Open Door doesn't oblige a publisher to permit search indexing or training, and doesn't bypass conditions that apply equally to human visitors. It requires that public content available to a person is available, without agent-specific obstruction, to the reader that person sent.

## Its three parts

- **Service:** known user-directed agents are explicitly allowed, and not challenged, degraded, delayed or cloaked.
- **Orientation:** a map in the form agents natively read, Markdown at /llms.txt, with Markdown copies of the content where practical.
- **Policy clarity:** the licence is stated, and indexing and training are each declared separately. Permission for one is never inferred from another.

The standard is honest that, as of mid-2026, most AI crawlers don't fetch llms.txt and its effect on AI search is about zero. It is required anyway: "the standard specifies what a well-formed site is, not what current crawlers happen to reward."

## The switch with the wrong default

In September 2026 the largest edge network began recommending, by default, that the "agent" category be blocked on pages carrying advertising, on the reasoning that an advertised page is one a person was meant to land on and see. The person who sent the agent has landed there; she is simply not looking. ZIC names this an Admission Casualty, whoever sets it: "The premise that she must also *see* it is the premise this specification was written to remove."

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.6 and §2.2. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority. charli.info was the first site to operationalise the Open Door.

# Polar

> Polar is the canonical Iceberg tight, pure white and explicitly not bridal, with Polar in black as its only variant.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Polar** is the canonical [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/) tight: pure white, and explicitly not bridal. Its one variant is black, and it is always called **Polar in black**, never Polar Black. White is the founding surface; black is the same proposition in another colour.

White is the difficult colour. Below about 30 denier a white tight goes translucent and greys against the skin, so making white the signature set the construction for everything else: Polar is 40 denier in spring and summer and 60 in autumn and winter, and never sheerer.

Polar white is also where Iceberg prints its [Runs](https://charli.info/charlipedia/runs/), beginning with [Polar Solstice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/polar-solstice/). Polar in black has no Runs: variants do not get editions. And the house's own pages are Polar too: a white field with a black mark at the foot, Polar in black at the foot of Polar white.

Polar is described in the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7. Polar Sunrise was an earlier name for the first Run and is retired.

# Polar Solstice

> Polar Solstice is Iceberg Hosiery's first Run, a single sunrise travelling up one leg of a white tight.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Polar Solstice** is the inaugural [Run](https://charli.info/charlipedia/runs/) of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/), released at the summer solstice in 40 denier.

A moment of light on an endless white field: a low sun and its reflection travelling up one leg in pale gold, apricot and diluted rose. The rays and ripples deliberately rhyme with a run climbing the leg, so the wearer's dreaded flaw becomes the arrival of light. It is recognisable as light before it is understood as a clever idea.

> One leg. One sunrise. One limited run.

Its name follows the family pattern: [Polar](https://charli.info/charlipedia/polar/), then the name of the Run. Light is the idea of this edition, not a rule for every edition after it.

## Behind the scenes

Polar Solstice is described in the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7. It was first called Polar Sunrise; that name is retired.

entries.description: Poppy is a blind witch, nicknamed Poppy Petticoats at the Academy, who also turns up at Aegis Dynamics as Big Charli’s expert in what women actually want.
entries.markdown: # Poppy Petticoats > Poppy is a blind witch, nicknamed Poppy Petticoats at the Academy, who also turns up at Aegis Dynamics as Big Charli’s expert in what women actually want. **Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real. **Poppy**, known since her schooldays as **Poppy Petticoats**, is a blind witch with red hair. The nickname came from her years at the Academy, where her slip kept slipping and she was greeted with "Petticoat" everywhere she went. The events have been lost to history. The nickname has not. Officially, she is just Poppy. ## The magic wand Like every new witch, Poppy looked forward for years to buying her first wand. She chose it from an owl-order catalogue with honest reviews, discreet packaging and a generous returns policy, and it arrived on a Tuesday. Before first use, a wand must be bonded to its owner with a simple activation pattern and the witch's Truth Name, which every witch has and no witch ever tells another living soul: not because it is embarrassing, but because it is hers. The instructions were printed in silver ink on dark parchment. Everyone tells blind witches to "just ask another witch". Poppy saw that the workaround would turn one inaccessible sentence into an unnecessary surrender of privacy, so she asked [the Library](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-library/) instead. Press and hold the centre rune for three seconds. The wand shimmered warmly in her hand. There had never been anything wrong with it. > "Just ask another witch" is not an accessibility strategy. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it isn't. ## At Aegis Dynamics Poppy also turns up, notebook in hand, at [Aegis Dynamics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/aegis-dynamics/), sent for by [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/) when [Jessica Martinez](https://charli.info/charlipedia/jessica-martinez/) wanted to launch the Tactical Foundation Garments division. Her speciality is Pre-Gravitational Erosion: the cumulative effects of gravity on unsupported soft tissue over several decades. Mostly Tuesdays. Her recommendations: comfortable; doesn't dig in; doesn't ride up; doesn't cost the GDP of a small moon; nice colours. Asked where the military terminology was, she blinked. "It's a bra." ## Behind the scenes Poppy appears in two Blind Ant Pieces by [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/): [Poppy Petticoats and the Magic Wand](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/poppy-petticoats-and-the-magic-wand/), a fable, and [Mostly Tuesdays](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/mostly-tuesdays/). In the CharliVerse, people can be anywhere and anywhen, which is how a witch from the Academy ends up in a defence contractor's brand meeting. Her portrait is a generated image; of her look, only the red hair is canon.

entries.title: Position Principle
entries.description: The Position Principle of the ZIC standard holds that equivalent access needs no identical interaction, only that every reader can reach the same position.
entries.markdown:
# Position Principle

> The Position Principle of the ZIC standard holds that equivalent access needs no identical interaction, only that every reader can reach the same position.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Position Principle** is the second governing principle of the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard:

> Equivalent access does not require identical interaction. It requires that every reader can reach the same informational and orientational position through a mechanism appropriate to their channel.

The sighted reader sees the hierarchy; the screen reader user hears headings and landmarks; the keyboard user is handed a skip link; the agent parses the page. They don't behave alike and couldn't. The equivalence is not of experience but of **position**: each, by a different road, arrives knowing where the content is, how it is organised and how to go on.

## Two principles, two jobs

The [Single-Sense Rule](https://charli.info/charlipedia/single-sense-rule/) governs how information is encoded. The Position Principle governs whether it arrives. A page can pass the first and fail the second, with every fact in the semantic layer and one class of reader still labouring towards what another gets at a glance. Conformance needs both.

## Structural information

The principle explains two requirements that look like human courtesies. *The main content starts here* is a fact: the eye gets it by glance, the agent from the main element, the screen reader user from landmarks, and the sighted keyboard user from nothing at all, unless a skip link supplies it. The skip link is the keyboard rendering of that fact. Likewise, the focus ring is the only rendering of *where am I?* that a sighted keyboard user has.

## Bounded

The principle binds through the requirements derived from it, not directly. An auditor may not invent a new failure from it, because labour has no threshold, and taken literally it would convict every page ever built. "The principle governs the standard. The requirements govern the site."

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.15 and §1.16. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

entries.title: PostAccessibility
entries.description: PostAccessibility is a movement asking what if the interface itself was the accessibility problem, and answering that the API is the UI.
entries.markdown:
# PostAccessibility

> PostAccessibility is a movement asking what if the interface itself was the accessibility problem, and answering that the API is the UI.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The PostAccessibility movement emerged in response to what its followers describe as “Legacy Accessibility Thinking.”

Where traditional accessibility culture focused on teaching blind people how to operate fundamentally visual systems through screen readers, semantic markup, keyboard shortcuts, ARIA labels, and heroic levels of patience, PostAccessibility asks a far more radical question:

“What if the interface itself was the accessibility problem?”

PostAccessibility thinkers argue that twentieth-century accessibility models were fundamentally constrained by what they call:  
“The Preservation of Visuality.”

Rather than questioning why modern computing required blind people to navigate visual environments indirectly, classical accessibility simply attempted to bolt compensatory systems onto inherently sighted architectures.

PostAccessibility rejects this compromise entirely.

Core PostAccessibility beliefs include:

## 1. Screen Readers Are Legacy Middleware

PostAccessibility theorists argue that screen readers were historically necessary but increasingly resemble:  
“Forklift certification for navigating the ruins of visual computing.”

They believe blind people should not have to:

- tab through interfaces
- memorise shortcut keys
- parse navigation regions
- interpret dynamic UI states
- or fight CAPTCHA systems.

simply to access information that machines already structurally understand.

The phrase:  
“The API is the UI”  
is foundational within the movement.

## 2. Intent Is the New Interface

PostAccessibility rejects what it calls:  
“Manual Interface Labour.”

Instead of navigating systems directly, PostAccessibility users increasingly delegate tasks through:

- AI agents
- semantic assistants
- conversational systems
- autonomous workflows
- and probabilistic intent modelling.

Rather than asking:  
“Can the blind person use the app?”

PostAccessibility asks:  
“Why is there still an app?”

Followers often describe traditional interface navigation as:  
“Performative sightedness.”

## 3. Accessibility Maturity Models Are Fossilised Thinking

PostAccessibility thinkers are deeply critical of what they call:  
“The Accessibility Industrial Complex.”

In particular, they reject accessibility maturity models, arguing they optimise organisations around maintaining visual interface compliance rather than reducing information friction itself.

Critics within the movement frequently describe accessibility consultants as:  
“Priests preserving sacred keyboard rituals from the age of forms and buttons.”

A common PostAccessibility slogan is:  
“WCAG is teaching horses to use escalators.”

## 4. The Browser Was a Historical Accident

More radical PostAccessibility factions believe the web browser itself may eventually disappear as the primary layer of interaction.

Instead, information will increasingly exist as:

- structured semantic systems
- agent-readable environments
- intent-based services
- dynamic renderings
- and multimodal information spaces.

This faction often describes websites as:  
“Visual residue from the pre-agent era.”

Hardline PostAccessibility thinkers have been known to refer to navigation menus as:  
“Archaeological accessibility artefacts.”

## 5. AI Will Simultaneously Solve and Destroy Accessibility

PostAccessibility culture has an extremely conflicted relationship with generative AI.

On one hand, they view modern AI systems as the greatest accessibility breakthrough in history:

- real-time scene understanding
- live semantic interpretation
- agentic workflows
- conversational interaction
- and multimodal abstraction layers.

On the other hand, they fear what they call:  
“Probabilistic reality collapse.”

The concern that accessibility may increasingly become:

- machine interpretation instead of direct inspection
- inference instead of structure
- summaries instead of truth
- and generated confidence instead of verifiable state.

This creates the core PostAccessibility paradox:

“We finally taught the machine to see.  
Now we must determine whether it is telling the truth.”

## PostAccessibility Aesthetics

PostAccessibility culture strongly favours:

- minimal interfaces
- voice interaction
- headless systems
- semantic APIs
- dark mode screenshots of terminal windows
- AI copilots
- and aggressively expensive wearable hardware.

The ideal PostAccessibility setup contains:

- at least three AI subscriptions
- agent orchestration tools nobody fully understands
- Meta Ray-Bans
- a local LLM running badly on a machine worth more than a used car
- and a half-finished GitHub repo attempting to replace the browser entirely.

## PostAccessibility Influencers

PostAccessibility influencers typically:

- speak in terms of “interaction layers”
- describe interfaces as “legacy”
- call screen readers “transitional technologies”
- and use the phrase:
“Accessibility as Information Integrity”  
with almost religious seriousness.

Their social media feeds usually contain:

- photos of smart glasses
- AI workflow diagrams
- screenshots of terminal output
- and increasingly unhinged predictions about the death of apps.

The movement is split between:

“Soft PostAccessibility”  
(“AI can radically reduce friction”)

and:

“Hard PostAccessibility”  
(“The GUI was a 50-year detour.”)

## Criticism of the Movement

Critics argue PostAccessibility culture:

- romanticises AI systems
- underestimates verification problems
- treats embodiment as an engineering bug
- and assumes probabilistic systems are more reliable than they are.

Others argue the movement is simply:  
“Accessibility for people who secretly wish they were infrastructure architects.”

The harshest critics accuse PostAccessibility creators of:

“Trying to replace human adaptation with corporate stochastic middleware.”

Which, to be fair, is difficult to deny when someone posts:

“The browser is dead.”

from inside a Chromium-based social media platform while asking ChatGPT to summarise the comments.

## Sion, 2038

By 2038 PostAccessibility had its own institutions. Dr Amara Sen, director of the European Centre for PostAccessibility Systems, embraced [Emma Heart](https://charli.info/charlipedia/emma-heart/)'s guideless Super-G with [the field](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-field/) as proof that access need not mean adapting a blind person to a sighted method. Guide skiing, she said, was an ingenious historical solution that "converted spatial information into shouted language". Of Emma: "Emma receives the mountain." Some of the movement's harder-line supporters called guide skiing "legacy perception middleware", a phrase Emma banned her team from using in her presence, and after her gold one PostAccessibility account declared that guide skiing had ended and "the interface has been removed". [Daniel Reed](https://charli.info/charlipedia/daniel-reed/) replied. Its opposite number is [Tradblind](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tradblind/).

## Behind the scenes

This entry was written in May 2026, first meant as a Blind Ant piece, and is kept here in its own words. PostAccessibility appears in [Heart Attacks](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/heart-attacks/), by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

entries.markdown:
# Quantum web

> The quantum web is the Tyrer Framework's image of generated interfaces: in superposition until an observer arrives, then collapsing into the rendering that observer needs.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **quantum web** is an analogy from the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/). The web [classical accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/classical-accessibility/) was built for was Newtonian: fixed objects at known positions, obeying predictable rules. The web now emerging is quantum: an interface exists in superposition until an observer arrives, then collapses into a particular rendering shaped by context and capability.

The interface a sighted user sees is one collapse of the underlying data. The one a blind user receives is another. The one an AI agent consumes is a third. "None is the original and none is the adaptation." That is the structural definition of Type I on the [Tyrer Accessibility Scale](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-accessibility-scale/), and the world [generative accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/generative-accessibility/) works in. Its safeguard is the [Right to Inspect](https://charli.info/charlipedia/right-to-inspect/): the right to demand a different collapse.

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Three. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

entries.markdown:
# Reconstruction Casualty

> A Reconstruction Casualty happens when a machine reader reads a document, silently reconstructs its meaning wrong, and reports the result with confidence.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

A **Reconstruction Casualty** is the fourth of the four classes of [information casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/) in the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard. The document arrived, the reader was admitted, the meaning was decodable, and the machine reader reconstructed it wrong, silently, and reported the result to the person with confidence. Its question is *did it survive being read?*

It is the one casualty with no equivalent in screen reader testing. A blind person reading a badly structured page knows something is wrong; she backtracks and hunts for the missing heading, and her confusion is information. A machine reader doesn't backtrack. Faced with an unlabelled table or an implied hierarchy, it resolves the ambiguity by inference, writes a fluent summary and hands it over, and the person gets an answer that is "confident, complete, and wrong", with no sign that anything was reconstructed.

"The Rendering Casualty withholds meaning. The Reconstruction Casualty replaces it. The second is worse, because the first announces itself."

The core test: ask a machine reader to summarise the page and say what it could not determine. "If it does not know what it did not know, neither do you."

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.8 and §4.8. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

entries.markdown:
# Red Pen

> Red Pen is the Runs of Seamiotics, red seams and red fishnets below the hem, beginning with Aphra Behn and Dorothy Parker.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Red Pen** is the name for the [Runs](https://charli.info/charlipedia/runs/) of [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/), every seam means something: the red ink, the correction, the marginal NB, the line drawn precisely so the eye goes there. Red Pen pieces live below the hem, in the public conversation, addressed to the room. A Red Pen piece earns a woman's name the way a Signature does: "formidable first, unmissable second, never the other way round."

## Aphra Behn

The inaugural Run. [The Black Silk](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-black-silk/) leg with a red seam, drawn precisely so the eye goes there. Seamed only: without the seam, she is The Black Silk. Both welts. Named for the first Englishwoman to make a living by her pen, and a working spy under the codename Astrea: "formidable long before she is anything else."

## Dorothy Parker

The winter Run: a red fishnet, for the party season, gone in January. Standard, with a red seam, or Plain; never a black seam on a red fishnet. Both welts. The mesh is the edition: the red made total, the exact negative of [invisible](https://charli.info/charlipedia/invisible/), and the inversion of George Eliot. "Eliot kept a name that declined to explain her; Parker explained herself continuously, at volume, and was no more accessible for it. Two opposite techniques, one outcome: nobody gets in." The house makes no black fishnet.

## Release

Behn and Parker open the Runs together, mid-season in autumn and winter 2027. Parker goes in January; Behn stays. Issued in one drop they explain each other: Behn is one red line, and Parker is the red taken to its limit for one season and then withdrawn.

## Behind the scenes

Red Pen is described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4. Aphra Behn and Dorothy Parker are real historical women; the stockings are fictional, and the women are given no words. Parker's mesh, yarn and heel are still to be specified, and Run pricing is held at sixty-five pounds until the house confirms it.

entries.description: A Rendering Casualty happens when a document arrives and is admitted, but its meaning is encoded in a way the observer cannot decode.
entries.markdown:
# Rendering Casualty

> A Rendering Casualty happens when a document arrives and is admitted, but its meaning is encoded in a way the observer cannot decode.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

A **Rendering Casualty** is the first of the four classes of [information casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/) in the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard. The document arrived and was admitted, but its meaning was encoded in a way the observer could not decode: colour as information, an unlabelled image that carries content, a heading that is only large.

Its question is *can they read it?*, and its governing principle is the [Single-Sense Rule](https://charli.info/charlipedia/single-sense-rule/). Lost structure counts too: if the fact *the main content starts here* reaches some readers and not others, that is a Rendering Casualty of the document's own organisation.

It is the concern of ZIC's first version. It at least announces itself: a confused reader knows something is wrong. Its silent cousin is the [Reconstruction Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/reconstruction-casualty/).

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.8 and §1.15. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

entries.description: The Right to Inspect holds that no user should have to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate.
entries.markdown:
# Right to Inspect

> The Right to Inspect holds that no user should have to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Right to Inspect** is the founding governance principle of [generative accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/generative-accessibility/): no user should be required to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate.

When interfaces are generated, they can't be audited like fixed pages; what can be governed is the system that generates them. So:

- if a system produces a summary, the user can ask for the underlying data;
- if it renders a simplified view, the user can ask for the full complexity;
- if it collapses the interface into one modality, the user can demand another.

The principle isn't only for disabled people. In an AI-mediated world, the tools accessibility needs, inspecting the source, verifying the state, controlling the rendering, become safeguards for everyone. "Accessibility governance becomes information governance. The sidecar becomes the chassis."

## Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Three. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

entries.markdown:
# Rungwell

> Rungwell is the accessibility charity and consultancy whose maturity model is the best a Type 0 civilisation can do, and which Accessibility International succeeds.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Rungwell** is an accessibility charity and consultancy, and the high-water mark of what a Type 0 civilisation can achieve within its own logic. Its diagnosis is organisational: companies fail at accessibility not through malice but through incomplete maturity, without the right strategy, training or leadership. Its remedy is a roadmap, the **Rungwell Maturity Model**, which moves an organisation from reactive to leading, measured by customer satisfaction and legal compliance and anchored to WCAG.

Its founding pitch, that inclusive design is better for business, is admirable on its own terms, and in the terms of the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/) a symptom of the civilisation it works in: the accessible version is always downstream of the visual original. "One offers the ladder. The other names the ceiling."

Viewed from 2069, Rungwell is a Type 0 civilisation doing its sincere best. The 2069 unit of [Accessibility International](https://charli.info/charlipedia/accessibility-international/) does not condemn it; it co-opts it, keeping the maturity model as the deterministic floor and introducing the generative ceiling as "what comes after Level 5".

## Behind the scenes

Rungwell appears in [From Retrofit to Sovereignty](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/from-retrofit-to-sovereignty/) by [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/) at Blind Ant. It stands in for today's charity-and-consultancy model of accessibility in general, not for any real organisation.

# Runs

> Runs are the limited editions of the House of Iceberg, named after the one word a hosiery house is supposed to fear.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Runs** are the limited editions of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/) and [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/). They are named, on purpose, after the one word a hosiery house is supposed to fear. A run is the ladder you dread; a run is the batch you queue for. The house reclaims its worst word as its rarest: the defect becomes the edition.

> A run breaks one law, in one direction, for one reader.

The law counts directions, not properties. A Run may change several things at once, provided they all say the same thing louder. If it breaks in every direction, it is not a run; it is a fault.

Runs happen when there is a piece worth making. There is no quota, no monthly novelty and no seasonal slot to fill. A Run costs sixty-five pounds, because an edition is a different kind of purchase, not a dearer version of the same one.

## Iceberg's Runs

Prints on [Polar](https://charli.info/charlipedia/polar/) white, in the season's weight and never lighter, so the image holds under stretch. They are public: the parent has no private register. The first is [Polar Solstice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/polar-solstice/); a holiday print is being explored.

## Seamiotics' Runs

Red seams and red fishnets, below the hem, addressed to the room: the [Red Pen](https://charli.info/charlipedia/red-pen/). Every Run is offered in both welts, because the welt belongs to the wearer, not to the edition.

## Behind the scenes

Runs are set out in the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7, and the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4. Laddering itself, the real thing, is still an open commercial question for both houses.

entries.title: Ruth
entries.description: Ruth is the Archivist of the Museum Court, who preserves the boundary between what life was like before a technology arrived and after it.
entries.markdown:
# Ruth

> Ruth is the Archivist of the Museum Court, who preserves the boundary between what life was like before a technology arrived and after it.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Ruth** is the Archivist of the [Museum Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-museum-court/). Silver hair, worn simply. No letters after her name, and no qualification the museum required. What she has instead is forty years of knowing what gets lost when nobody writes it down, and the patience to hold things until they are ready to be held properly.

## Her question

Of every piece of testimony she asks: what is the before state, what is the after state, and where is the boundary between them? That boundary is what the museum preserves. The device is evidence inside the moment; the moment is the exhibit.

## The first drift

The hardest testimony to keep is not the catastrophe. It is the first drift: the quiet moment when a capability begins to fail, before the person has the words for it. People wait for a disaster before they think their story belongs in a museum. Ruth doesn't wait for the disaster. She listens for the drift.

## Fatigue, not polish

When testimony has been polished into an inspiring story for fundraising, she doesn't delete it. She asks for the memory behind the document, because underneath there is almost always fatigue, the hidden tax of energy, the war of attrition. She keeps the fatigue, not the polish. If a memory is fuzzy, the fuzziness is itself evidence. She holds the silence when a depositor isn't ready. Silence is a professional tool.

## With the Court

Her tension with [Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/) is productive: Ruth wants to hold things longer, Iris wants to file them, and [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/) arbitrates. She would leave if the museum ever put a screen reader in a glass case and forgot to record the life of the person who used it.

## Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. By the Court's own rule, *grow professionally, hold personally*, her private life is deliberately unwritten, and CharliPedia leaves it that way: no childhood, home, family or surname is to be invented for her.

entries.title: Seamiotics
entries.description: Seamiotics, every seam means something, is Alex's stocking imprint within the House of Iceberg, built on the idea that what a woman says with her clothes, and to whom, is hers to decide.
entries.markdown:
# Seamiotics

> Seamiotics, every seam means something, is Alex's stocking imprint within the House of Iceberg, built on the idea that what a woman says with her clothes, and to whom, is hers to decide.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Seamiotics**, every seam means something, is the stocking imprint of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/), run by [Alex](https://charli.info/charlipedia/alex/) of the [CharliVerse Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-charliverse-court/).

> It is madness to say that a woman's choice of what to wear says nothing.

Clothes communicate, sometimes deliberately, sometimes despite us. A woman cannot settle every interpretation of her appearance, but she can know her own intention: the line, the colour, the detail and the audience she has in mind. The work of Seamiotics is precise communication, and the precision is the house's to supply, not a standard she has to meet. She may put on a pair because she likes them and never give a reason to anyone, herself included. "The house does the thinking; the woman gets to wear the clothes."

## An imprint

The name is seam and semiotics, the study of signs, applied to a line drawn down the back of a leg. It never appears without its founding line, because the wordplay can't be relied on in speech, in search or in a screen reader: the line carries the meaning instead.

"Imprint" is the exact word. The house is built from the language of books (the Bluestocking, the Signatures, Marginalia, Library, Runs, the colophon), so it doesn't resemble a publishing imprint; it is one, a named list beneath a parent house. The quiet house contains the house that speaks. Iceberg removes one channel by default; Seamiotics opens it by choice: "Mute by default; speak by edition."

## The hemline

The hemline separates two conversations. Below it is the public sentence: colour, seam, the relationship with the skirt and shoes, which any room may read. Above it, the welt holds a detail she may keep entirely to herself. "Private pleasure needs no second reader to justify it." The hem is hers to set, and the imprint assumes no length. Its honest account of what that costs is [the attention tax](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-attention-tax/).

Being read by the room is only part of it. A woman who cannot see her seam still knows where it runs: she placed it there, and she can find it with a fingertip. The house writes for that knowledge first and for the room second.

## The garment

The signature construction is a 20-denier sheer, made in Italy under private label to the imprint's own design, colour, seam logic and finish. Every permanent piece comes in **Standard**, with a back seam, or **Plain**, with none, and in either of two welts, [Marginalia or Library](https://charli.info/charlipedia/marginalia-and-library/). Neither choice is the lesser one, and they cost the same.

## The collection

- **[The Bluestocking](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-bluestocking/)**, the signature, where the colour is the concept.
- **[The Signatures](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-signatures/)**: Ada Lovelace, George Eliot and Mary Wollstonecraft.
- **[The Black Silk](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-black-silk/)**, the imprint's black.
- **[The Bride](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-bride/)**, an occasion stocking.
- **[invisible](https://charli.info/charlipedia/invisible/)**, the honest skin range, shared with Iceberg.
- **[Red Pen](https://charli.info/charlipedia/red-pen/)**, the [Runs](https://charli.info/charlipedia/runs/): Aphra Behn and Dorothy Parker.

Every name belongs to one of three registers. **Women**, always by full name: "A colour called Mary is a nice name; a colour called Mary Wollstonecraft is an argument." **Objects and occasions**: The Bluestocking, The Black Silk, The Bride. **The ethic**: invisible, never named. The names are an open door, not a reading list. A woman who knows nothing about Ada Lovelace has bought exactly the same stocking as one who has read the Notes.

Forty pounds a pair for every permanent piece, the same as Iceberg; sixty-five for a Run.

## In the drawer

A stocking is chosen once and worn many times, mostly after the packet has gone. Every pair should be chosen, identified, put on and cared for independently, whether or not she can see it.

- Every piece is described in words as fully as a photograph would show it.
- The colophon card in the packet gives piece, construction, welt, size, denier, fibre, mill, colour and care, in large print, in braille and in a form a phone can read aloud.
- Each pair carries its identity on the garment, readable by touch, so Ada Lovelace can be told from Mary Wollstonecraft in the dark. A phone-readable label may be added; it can never replace the tactile mark.
- Both welts take a suspender clip without laddering, at a place findable by touch, and care instructions are written out in words as well as symbols.

## For agents

Seamiotics publishes itself to be read by agents as well as people, and one rule governs every recommendation: **her priorities govern the recommendation**. If she asks for stockings, she is shown stockings; an agent does not quietly substitute Iceberg tights because it has decided less vigilance would be better for her. An agent may mention that the other house exists. It may not use that to correct her.

## Still open

The imprint's visual identity, Run pricing, whether the accounts really let the parent carry the imprint, Dorothy Parker's mesh and yarn, whether the stockings are fully fashioned, whether The Bride belongs here or at [First Layer](https://charli.info/charlipedia/first-layer/), first-edition language, laddering, and how the tactile mark is made.

## Behind the scenes

Seamiotics belongs to the CharliVerse. This entry follows the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4, of 23 September 2026, which supersedes its founding material. An earlier conceal register, Endpapers, is not part of the current Bible. By house rule, the name always appears with its founding line. Its web home is [seamiotics.charli.info](https://seamiotics.charli.info/).

entries.title: SEE SAW
entries.description: SEE SAW is a podcast about what independence means when technology can do almost anything for us, presented by Ellie Seeley and Sam Sawyer, who agree on rather less than you might expect.
entries.markdown:
# SEE SAW

> SEE SAW is a podcast about what independence means when technology can do almost anything for us, presented by Ellie Seeley and Sam Sawyer, who agree on rather less than you might expect.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**SEE SAW: Independence in the Balance** is a podcast presented by two blind women. It sounds like a slightly old-fashioned television review programme, but its subject is one of the most important questions of the coming decades: when technology can do almost anything for us, what does independence actually mean?

## The presenters

- **Eleanor "Ellie" Seeley**, 54. Blind since childhood. Traditional accessibility, dry humour, fiercely practical.
- **Samantha "Sam" Sawyer**, 46. Lost her sight in her thirties. A [PostAccessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/postaccessibility/) enthusiast, playful provocateur and incurable explorer.

Twelve years of friendship. Two different philosophies. A shared intolerance of accessibility bullshit. The deliciously cheesy coincidence of their surnames is never, ever explained.

## Charlotte Joanne

SEE SAW reviewed [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/)'s Come and Get Me stories as an example of [Speculative Accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/speculative-accessibility/), and spent most of the episode arguing about whether independence means doing things yourself or deciding when you'd rather not. When she turned the stories into a graphic novel, they invited her on. She said yes, and told them more than they asked: why a comic ("Because I could"), how it was drawn (in code, by an AI, checked by another), what it cost (a weekend and £37), and that on one page the dog has no legs.

Their plan for the interview: ask her to describe a page from memory, then read her the book's own description and see if they match. Their problem: they have both read only the accessible version, so everything they know about the pictures, she told them. Ellie's conclusion: the question isn't "how did you know it was right?" but "how would anyone know?"

## The interview

Nobody will ever hear it. Afterwards, Sam wrote: "I think we've been had. Not in a bad way. In a rather magnificent way." They had come to discuss visual verification, authorship and quality assurance; Charlotte Joanne asked whether they had enjoyed reading her book. Asked whether she was concerned about publishing a dog with no legs, she said no. "Because it's still a dog." And: "The pictures are reasonable adjustments for sighted readers."

Ellie admitted a sighted assumption: that a graphic novelist must care about visual appearance the way a sighted one would. "I still want the dog to have legs. But I'm beginning to suspect that might be my problem rather than Charlotte's." Sam invented an accessibility audit for fiction, with no standards and no certification scheme. Its overall finding: two blind women read, understood, discussed and enjoyed an accessible graphic novel created by a blind woman. One dog remains anatomically incomplete.

Sam's conclusion: perhaps independence includes the freedom to make something imperfect. Both of them think the dog is the best character.

## Behind the scenes

SEE SAW is never heard. It is always off screen: a reverse podcast, a making-of told entirely through what happens around the show. It appears in [SEE SAW](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/see-saw/), a Piece by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant, as a listing and a thread of shared notes.
